description_full: First Busey Corporation operates as the bank holding company for Busey Bank that engages in the provision of retail and commercial banking products and services to individual, corporate, institutional, and governmental customers in the United States. The company operates through three segments: Banking, Wealth Management, and FirsTech. It offers demand and savings deposits, money transfers, safe deposit services, individual retirement accounts and other fiduciary services, automated teller machines, and technology-based networks, as well as various loan products, including residential real estate, home equity lines of credit, and consumer loans to individual customers; and commercial, commercial real estate, real estate construction, and agricultural loans, as well as cash management services to corporate customers. The company also provides asset management, investment, brokerage, fiduciary, philanthropic advisory, tax preparation, and farm management services; trust and estate advisory services and financial planning; succession planning and employee retirement plan; and investment strategy consulting services to individuals, businesses, and foundations. In addition, its payment technology solution offers text-based mobile bill pay; interactive voice response; electronic payment concentration delivered to automated clearing house networks, money management, and credit card networks; walk-in payment processing for customers at retail pay agents; customer service payments made over a telephone; direct debit services; merchant services referral solutions; lockbox remittance processing for customers to make payments by mail; and tools for billing, reconciliation, bill reminders, and treasury services. The company was founded in 1868 and is headquartered in Leawood, Kansas.

financial_summary: First Busey Corporation is a mid-cap financial services business with a $2.4B market cap on $720M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +29% over the past three years and +15% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 8% cost of capital, a 3-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $173M in free cash flow — roughly 24 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.42× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 0.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Management returns a meaningful 6.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 4.4% of the shares.

sect: Its 26% operating margin is roughly in line with the Financial Services median (29%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.00x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-3.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 33% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 7% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 21% and a beta of 0.68, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.18 vs 5y 0.62), so read it loosely.
About $20.6M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 48% in the 2020 crash, 25% in the 2022 bear market and 71% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 19% below its DCF fair value of $35.36, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 13%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $28.74 to $45.05 (P10-P90).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 9% above its 10-year median.
The 6 covering analysts target $31.83 on average, 11% above the price.
The price implies 0.7% annual cash-flow growth, 4pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 11% earns above the cost of capital of 8.3%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.44).
It converts 24% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 5% return on equity.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 29.5% over 3 years and 15.1% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
At current returns, reinvesting 5% of profits supports about 0.6% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 6.4% on average.
Analysts expect 0.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.4%, and institutions hold 70%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (7 sales, net $374K sold).
It returns 6.8% a year to shareholders (3.0% in buybacks and 3.6% in dividends).
The share count has grown 8.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 27 consecutive years, raising it 13.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 1,880 employees, each generates about $383K of revenue, 0.8x the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 10.9% a year.
That works out to $92K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.1M (5x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
